metadata.note: Cleveland's rapid transit -- the RTA Rapid, four rail lines that reached the city from two completely separate origins. The Blue and Green Lines are the older half: interurban light rail built by the Van Sweringen brothers' Cleveland Interurban Railroad to sell lots in their Shaker Heights development, the Shaker Boulevard line opening December 17 1913 and the Moreland (later Van Aken) line April 11 1920. Cleveland Union Terminal opened in 1930 and gave them a grade-separated approach downtown alongside the steam railroads; the City of Shaker Heights bought the struggling lines on September 6 1944 and ran them itself as the Shaker Heights Rapid Transit. The Red Line is the newer half and the only true heavy-rail rapid transit: built by the Cleveland Transit System (formed 1942, when the city took over the Cleveland Railway Company), it opened March 15 1955 and is split here into its three construction stages, because the last of them is the line's claim to fame -- on November 15 1968 the Red Line reached Cleveland Hopkins Airport, making Cleveland the first city in the Western Hemisphere with direct rapid transit between downtown and its major airport. The Greater Cleveland RTA, established December 30 1974, took over both systems on September 5 1975. The Waterfront Line of 1996 is the newest and the least fortunate: suspended October 26 2020 over safety concerns, it returned September 10 2023 for Cleveland Browns games only, which is why it vanishes from the map between 2020 and 2023. Geometry is real GCRTA track alignment from the agency's own GTFS shapes; colours, end-to-end run times and modern headways come from the same feed.

metadata.not_yet_sourced: Only the 2026 segment's headway is real: it is counted from the GTFS feed. Every pre-2026 headway is an estimate -- no Cleveland Transit System, Shaker Heights Rapid Transit or early RTA timetable has been consulted, and the values do not reflect how much better service was in the 1920s or how much it deteriorated in the 1970s. The 1958 West Park extension is dated to the year only; the exact date was not verified. The Red Line is split into its three construction stages because station-level opening dates were available for it; the Blue and Green Lines are NOT split, even though both were built and extended in stages between 1913 and the 1920s, because per-stage dates were not researched -- each is drawn at its full modern extent from its opening year, which overstates how far out they reached at first. All geometry is modern GCRTA alignment and does not reflect the pre-1930 approach to downtown before Cleveland Union Terminal, the 1980-81 reconstruction of the Shaker lines to modern light-rail standards, or any station that has since moved or closed. The GTFS feed still schedules regular Waterfront Line service, which conflicts with the reported Browns-games-only operation; the feed's numbers are used for the 2026 segment regardless. Cleveland's extensive city streetcar network, abandoned in 1954, is not in this file.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
